sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Delhi Durbar of 1911**: Grand imperial assembly held on December 12, 1911, where King George V announced the annulment of the **Partition of Bengal** and the shifting of the capital from Calcutta to **Delhi**.
• **Administrative Reorganization**: Bengal was reunited under a **Governor-in-Council**, while Bihar and Orissa were carved out as a separate province, and Assam was placed under a separate Chief Commissioner.
• **Motivations for Annulment**: Relentless nationalist agitation, the unyielding **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement**, rising **revolutionary terrorism**, and the desire to curb growing political unrest before the Royal Visit.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The annulment exposed the inherent contradictions of British divide-and-rule tactics while deeply disappointing sections of the Muslim political elite who had benefited from the creation of Eastern Bengal and Assam.

items.definition: An opulent imperial gathering to mark the coronation of King George V and Queen Mary, serving as the platform for major imperial policy announcements.
The upgraded administrative structure for the reunited Bengal presidency, replacing the Lieutenant-Governorship to match Bombay and Madras.
Relocation of the imperial headquarters from Calcutta to Delhi to symbolize historical continuity and distance the government from the hotbed of nationalist radicalism.

The sense of betrayal felt by conservative Muslim leaders (who supported the 1905 partition for a Muslim-majority province) leading to a shift in Muslim League outlook towards greater pan-Islamism and anti-government stance.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Calcutta & Bengal Delta**: Reunited linguistic hub; witnessed celebration among nationalists but dissatisfaction among some Muslim leaders in East Bengal.
• **New Delhi (Imperial Capital Zone)**: Chosen for its strategic central location, imperial heritage, and distance from Calcutta's volatile political climate.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Administrative disruption, alienation of East Bengal Muslims who lost administrative leverage, and increased communal polarization.
• **Policy Interventions**: Creation of Dacca University (1921) later recommended by the Nathan Committee to compensate Muslims of East Bengal for educational losses resulting from the annulment.

items.title: Mnemonic for 1911 Royal Declarations
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'BAD' (Bengal Annulled, Delhi Capital, Bihar Separated).
• **Decoded Meaning**: B = Bengal Partition Annulled; A = Assam made separate Chief Commissionership; D = Delhi becomes capital / Bihar & Orissa separated.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly recalls the three core announcements made at the 1911 Delhi Durbar.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: 1905 Partition = Curzon's Divide; 1911 Annulment = Hardinge's Reversal.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently poses questions implying that the Partition of Bengal was annulled primarily to satisfy the Indian National Congress's moderate leadership completely. In reality, the annulment was done secretly and announced abruptly to check revolutionary terrorism and appease elite concerns, while simultaneously transferring the capital to Delhi to diminish Calcutta's political dominance.

Mains Value Addition: Analyze the annulment not merely as a victory for nationalism, but as a turning point that inadvertently sowed seeds of communal alienation in Eastern Bengal, steering the Muslim League toward a more assertive political posture in the subsequent decade.

keyTakeaways: The Annulment of the Partition of Bengal was announced in December 1911 at the Delhi Durbar by King George V.
It reunited Bengal under a Governor-in-Council while separating Bihar, Orissa, and Assam into distinct administrative units.
While it marked a monumental victory for Indian nationalist resistance, it left a legacy of communal estrangement among East Bengal Muslims.
